The following subsections explore each of the scenarios and how they compare to each other in more detail. 4.1.1 Uncontrolled Case This is the simplest case from a controller and site design perspective, and is treated as a baseline against which to compare the more sophisticated site controllers. In this case, the only control decision is made by the RCC operators based on the vehicles’ return SOC: If the SOC is more than or equal to 40%, then the vehicle is assigned a 25-kW EVSE. Otherwise, a 350-kW EVSE is 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. used. Once the vehicle is charging, its charge acceptance curve (CAC) dictates the power transferred to charge the battery; no dynamic EVSE power set point setting is performed, nor is any DER deployed. The time series from this scenario of main outputs—facility loads, net power demand from the grid, and grid capacity limit—are presented in Figure 12, while the aggregated results are in Table 4. In this case, around 8% of charging sessions are not completed, meaning 8% of the 750 vehicles do not reach 80% by their next rental pick, and the average SOC deficit is 13%. This deficit is due to both the EVSE assignment (certain EVs might be returned with SOC higher that 40% but have a very short dwell time) and the combination of a short dwell time and high energy requirement (certain sessions simply cannot be completed, even on a 350-kW EVSE). In addition to these limitations, a significant portion of the load exceeds the grid capacity ceiling, with the simulation net peak load amounting to 3.6 MW. To accommodate the peak load above the current ceiling, on-site distribution upgrades totaling more than $4.2 million might be required. Figure 12. Uncontrolled simulation results Table 4.
